lessons.title: Introduction to Computer Networks
lessons.overview: A computer network is a collection of interconnected devices (computers, servers, routers, switches) that can communicate and share resources. Networks are classified by size (LAN, MAN, WAN), topology (bus, star, ring, mesh), and protocol. Understanding network architecture is essential for any IT professional.
keyConcepts: Network: A group of connected devices that share data and resources
LAN (Local Area Network): Small geographic area (office, building) — Ethernet, Wi-Fi
MAN (Metropolitan Area Network): City-wide — cable TV network
WAN (Wide Area Network): Large geographic area — Internet
PAN (Personal Area Network): Very small (Bluetooth, USB)
Topology: Physical or logical arrangement of devices (Bus, Star, Ring, Mesh, Tree)
Protocol: Set of rules governing communication (TCP, IP, HTTP, FTP)
Node: Any device on the network (computer, printer, router)
Bandwidth: Maximum data transfer rate (measured in bps, Kbps, Mbps, Gbps)
Latency: Time for data to travel from source to destination
formulas: Propagation Delay = Distance / Speed of Signal

rows: Single point of failure, limited length
Break in ring stops all communication

commonMistakes: Confusing LAN with WAN — LAN is local (building), WAN is wide (Internet)
Forgetting that protocols define rules, not physical connections
examTips: Draw each topology diagram clearly with labels
List advantages and disadvantages of each topology
Know the 4 network types by size: PAN < LAN < MAN < WAN
Define bandwidth, latency, throughput, and efficiency
practiceQuestions: What is a computer network? List its advantages.
Differentiate between LAN, MAN, and WAN.
What is a protocol? Give 5 examples.

lessons.title: OSI and TCP/IP Models
lessons.overview: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model is a 7-layer conceptual framework that standardizes network communication. Each layer has specific functions and protocols. The TCP/IP model is a simpler 4-layer model used in practice (the Internet runs on TCP/IP). Understanding these models is critical for network troubleshooting and design.
keyConcepts: OSI Model: 7 layers — Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
TCP/IP Model: 4 layers — Network Access, Internet, Transport, Application
Encapsulation: Each layer adds its own header to the data (PDU = Protocol Data Unit)
Physical Layer: Transmits raw bits over a medium (cables, wireless)
Data Link Layer: Node-to-node delivery, error detection (MAC addressing, switches)
Network Layer: Host-to-host delivery, routing (IP addressing, routers)
Transport Layer: End-to-end delivery, reliability (TCP, UDP, port numbers)
Session Layer: Establishes, manages, terminates sessions
Presentation Layer: Data translation, encryption, compression
Application Layer: User interface (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS)
formulas: OSI Layers (bottom to top): Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away
TCP/IP = OSI layers 1+2 → Network Access, Layer 3 → Internet, Layer 4 → Transport, Layers 5+6+7 → Application
PDU per layer: Bits (1) → Frames (2) → Packets (3) → Segments (4) → Data (5-7)
commonMistakes: Confusing the order of OSI layers (Physical is bottom, Application is top)
Mixing up which devices operate at which layer (switch = Layer 2, router = Layer 3)
Forgetting that TCP is reliable (connection-oriented) and UDP is unreliable (connectionless)
examTips: Use the mnemonic: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away (Physical → Application)
Draw the OSI model with all 7 layers, protocols, and devices
Compare TCP vs UDP: TCP = reliable, ordered, 3-way handshake; UDP = fast, no guarantee
Show how data is encapsulated as it moves down the layers
practiceQuestions: Explain the OSI model with all 7 layers and their functions.
Compare the OSI and TCP/IP models.
What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
Which devices operate at Layer 2 and Layer 3? Give examples.
Explain the process of data encapsulation in the OSI model.

lessons.title: IP Addressing and Subnetting
lessons.overview: An IP (Internet Protocol) address is a unique identifier assigned to each device on a network. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses (4 billion addresses), while IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses. IP addresses are divided into classes (A, B, C, D, E), and subnetting allows networks to be divided into smaller sub-networks for efficient address utilization.
keyConcepts: IPv4: 32-bit address written as 4 octets (e.g., 192.168.1.1)
IPv6: 128-bit address written as 8 groups of hex digits (e.g., 2001:0db8:85a3::)
IP Classes: A (1-126), B (128-191), C (192-223), D (multicast), E (experimental)
Subnet Mask: Defines network and host portions (e.g., 255.255.255.0 = /24)
Subnetting: Dividing a large network into smaller sub-networks
CIDR: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24)
Private IP Ranges: 10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x (not routable on Internet)
NAT: Network Address Translation — maps private IPs to public IPs
DHCP: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol — assigns IP addresses automatically
DNS: Domain Name System — maps domain names to IP addresses
formulas: Network Address = IP AND Subnet Mask
Broadcast Address = Network Address OR NOT(Subnet Mask)
Number of Subnets = 2^n (n = bits borrowed for subnetting)
Number of Hosts per Subnet = 2^h - 2 (h = host bits, -2 for network and broadcast)
CIDR: /n means n bits for network, (32-n) bits for hosts
commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract 2 from the host count (network + broadcast addresses)
Confusing network address with first usable host address
Not understanding that 127.x.x.x is loopback (localhost), not Class A
examTips: Memorize the class ranges: A (1-126), B (128-191), C (192-223)
For subnetting: identify borrowed bits, then use 2^n for subnets and 2^h-2 for hosts
Practice converting between decimal and binary for subnet masks
Know private IP ranges and what NAT does
practiceQuestions: What is an IP address? Explain IPv4 vs IPv6.
List the IP address classes with their ranges.
Given 192.168.1.0/26, find: number of subnets, hosts per subnet, network and broadcast addresses.
What is subnetting? Why is it used?
Explain NAT and DHCP with their purposes.
